dijkstra.title: How petgraph::algo::dijkstra() works
dijkstra.description: Shortest distances from one node, settling the closest unvisited node first.

note.text: shortest distance from A to every node

slides.caption: dijkstra() keeps a best-known distance for every node. It starts with 0 for A and "unknown" (∞) for the rest.
A is the closest unsettled node (0): settle it. Through its edges, B can be reached in 4 and C in 1.
C (1) is now the closest unsettled node: settle it. Via C, B costs 1 + 2 = 3, better than 4. D costs 1 + 5 = 6.
B (3) is next: settle it. Via B, D costs 3 + 1 = 4, better than 6.
D (4) is the last node. A settled node never gets a better distance later, because all weights are ≥ 0.
dijkstra() returns a HashMap from node to distance (sorted here by name). Pass Some(goal) to stop early. Negative weights need bellman_ford().

toposort.title: How petgraph::algo::toposort() works
toposort.description: Orders the nodes so that every arrow points forward; a cycle is an error.

note.text: an arrow X → Y means "X must come before Y"

slides.caption: Think of tasks with dependencies: A before B and C, and both B and C before D. toposort() finds an order that respects every arrow.
A has no arrows coming in, so nothing has to happen before it: it goes first.
With A done, B and C are both free. Either order is valid; petgraph's depth-first search places C here.
Then B.
D needs both B and C, so it comes last. Every arrow now points from an earlier to a later node.
toposort() returns Ok(Vec<NodeIndex>). If the graph has a cycle there is no valid order, and it returns Err(Cycle(node)).

is-cyclic-directed.title: How petgraph::algo::is_cyclic_directed() works
is-cyclic-directed.description: Finds out whether following the arrows can lead back to where you started.

note.text: edges A → B, B → C, C → A

slides.caption: is_cyclic_directed() walks the graph depth-first and remembers which nodes are on the current path.
Start at A. A is on the path.
Follow A → B. B joins the path.
Follow B → C.
C → A leads to a node that is still on the current path. That arrow closes a loop: a cycle.

eq.text: A is already on the path → cycle

slides.caption: is_cyclic_directed(&g) is true. Without the arrow C → A it would be false, and toposort() would succeed.

bfs-next.title: How Bfs::next() works
bfs-next.description: Visits a graph breadth-first: all neighbours before the neighbours' neighbours.

note.text: bfs = Bfs::new(&g, a); a FIFO queue decides the order

slides.caption: Each call to next() returns one node. Bfs keeps a queue: nodes found first are visited first.
next() returns A, the start. Its neighbours B and C join the queue.
B comes out of the queue first; its neighbour D is added at the back.
C is next, still at distance 1 from A. Its neighbour E goes to the back.
Only then the nodes at distance 2: D, then E.
Level by level: A, then B and C, then D and E. In an unweighted graph BFS reaches every node by a shortest path.

note.text: result: A, B, C, D, E

dfs-next.title: How Dfs::next() works
dfs-next.description: Visits a graph depth-first: follows one path to its end before going back.

note.text: dfs = Dfs::new(&g, a); a stack (last in, first out) decides the order

slides.caption: Dfs keeps a stack. The node pushed last is visited next, so the walk goes deep before it goes wide.
next() returns A. Its neighbours are pushed: B, then C. C is on top.
C comes off the top. Its neighbour E is pushed on top of B.
E is visited next: the walk went all the way down A → C → E first.
That path is finished, so it backs up to B, and from B goes down to D.
Depth first: one branch completely (C, E), then the next (B, D). Which branch goes first depends on the order petgraph lists the edges.

note.text: result: A, C, E, B, D

connected-components.title: How petgraph::algo::connected_components() works
connected-components.description: Counts the separate groups of nodes that are linked to each other.

note.text: an undirected graph with edges A–B, B–C, D–E

slides.caption: Two nodes are in the same component when some path of edges links them.
Start at A: A–B and B–C link A, B and C. That is component 1.
D is not linked to any of them, so it starts component 2, together with E.
Every node now belongs to a component. (petgraph does this with a union-find structure, merging groups edge by edge.)
connected_components(&g) is 2. Adding an edge between C and D would make it 1.

astar.title: How petgraph::algo::astar() works
astar.description: Shortest path to a goal: Dijkstra guided by an estimate of the distance left.

note.text: each step costs 1; estimate = steps left to T, ignoring the hole

slides.caption: astar() ranks nodes by f = cost so far + estimate of the cost left. The estimate never overestimates, so the path found is a shortest one.
From S, both B and D cost 1, and both are 3 steps from T: f = 1 + 3 = 4.
They tie, so the search continues from one of them; petgraph picks D. D leads to G (f = 2 + 2).
G leads to H (3 + 1), and H to T (4 + 0). The f values never rose above 4, so no detour was needed.
T is reached with cost 4. Dijkstra would have spread out evenly in all directions; the estimate pulled the search towards T.
astar() returns Some((4, path)). The path along the top (S, B, C, F, T) is just as short; which one is returned depends on tie-breaking.

note.text: result: cost 4, path S → D → G → H → T
